Induction heads and their phase change

Heads learn to continue patterns by copying tokens following earlier matches. Olsson et al., 2022 ↗

OptimizationIn-context learning

Claims

SupportsLimitsChallenges
V2Induction heads emerge abruptly with early in-context learning gains and a loss bump 29160

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups reproduce abrupt induction-head emergence alongside gains in in-context learning or synthetic-task accuracy, but do not establish that a bump in training loss occurs at the same time. In the model Vanilla 1B, the sudden learning gain is absent on non-extractive samples, where the answer cannot be copied from context.

The phase-change claim's suggested status moves from contested to independently reproduced, with a stated limit. In one 1B model, the sudden in-context-learning gain did not appear when only positions that cannot be copied were scored; that single-seed result is now treated as a limit on the claim rather than a failed replication, pending a full re-read of the study.

Original resultOlsson et al., 2022 ↗

The original study tracked induction-head scores, loss at different positions in the context, and training loss in 34 decoder-only Transformers.

Induction heads appeared abruptly at approximately 2.5–5 billion training tokens, while the loss advantage for later tokens over earlier tokens rose from under 0.15 to roughly 0.4 nats. In the same window, the loss curve showed a small bump, described as a visibly steeper improvement.

Measurements and conditions (5)

In-context Learning and Induction Heads

34 decoder-only Transformer language models (aggregate) · Measured induction-head prefix matching over training using head activation evaluators. · Models: 34 models across four model series; Training window: approximately 2.5 to 5 billion tokens; small models described elsewhere as approximately 1 to 3 billion tokens

Formation of heads scoring as induction heads by prefix matching: Induction heads form abruptly in the same window as the in-context learning improvement. (baseline: Before the window, induction heads have not yet formed abruptly; one-layer models do not form them.)

34 decoder-only Transformer language models (aggregate) · Measured in-context learning as the loss difference between early and later context positions. · Token indices: 50th and 500th tokens; Training window: approximately 2.5 to 5 billion tokens

Key Concepts; Argument 1

Transformer language models (aggregate) · Observed the aggregate training loss curve during the induction-head and in-context-learning transition. · Training window: same early-training window as the reported phase change

Training loss curve: A small bump, described as a period of visibly steeper improvement; the paper calls it the only place in training where the loss is not convex. (baseline: Loss curve is described as monotonically decreasing in slope outside the transition.)

Argument 1

One-layer models (aggregate) · Measured induction-head scores, in-context learning, and training-loss behavior during training. · Depth: one layer; Architecture: standard, not smeared-key

Induction-head formation, in-context learning, and phase-change loss bump: Induction heads never form; in-context learning never substantially develops; the loss bump is absent. (baseline: Models with more than one layer show the reported transition.)

Argument 1; Argument 2; Model Details

Smeared-key models (aggregate) · Trained models with keys interpolated between the current token's key and the previous token's key using a trainable parameter. · Architecture: smeared key; Depth: one layer and two or more layers

Development and timing of in-context learning: In-context learning forms in one-layer models and forms earlier in two-layer and larger models. (baseline: Without smeared keys, the one-layer models do not develop the reported in-context learning transition; deeper models develop it later.)

Toy learning transitions depend on the setup 10 studies

In-context learning in toy settings can emerge abruptly, in stages or smoothly. Attention parametrisation, initialisation, task complexity and data size affect both the transition shape and whether learning succeeds.

  • Attention parametrisation changes regression learning from one abrupt drop to several staged drops. Yedi Zhang et al., 2025 ↗
  • Softmax attention jumps directly to copying, while linear attention first learns uniform pooling. Itay Lavie et al., 2026 ↗
  • Increasing regression dimension turns reliable in-context learning into seed-dependent jumps and eventual failure. Juwei Shen et al., 2026 ↗
Loss transitions do not uniquely identify induction 6 studies

Loss bumps and plateaus followed by drops also occur without attention-based induction heads. A change in training loss alone shows neither that a circuit formed nor that copying succeeded.

  • One-layer attention shows a loss bump despite flat multi-query associative recall accuracy; Mamba does too. Destiny Okpekpe et al., 2025 ↗
  • Recurrent neural networks show training-loss transitions on toy data despite lacking attention-based induction heads. Adam Shai et al., 2025 ↗
  • An N-gram-trained model shows loss plateaus and drops without developing induction heads. Jonas Rohweder et al., 2026 ↗
V4Induction behaviour recurs across model families, sizes, training runs and modalities 53110

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups reproduce induction behaviour across model families, sizes and training runs, and some report it in other architectures and modalities. How much induction behaviour causally contributes to performance varies with the model and test.

The suggested rating for this version changed from contested back to independently reproduced. One preprint found no working induction circuit in a small Pythia model, but other groups find induction heads with causal effects in that same model, so the result is now listed as a limit on scope.

Original resultOlsson et al., 2022 ↗

The original study measured induction-head prefix matching, a score for attending to continuations of earlier matching patterns, during training in 34 decoder-only Transformer language models from four model series.

Induction heads formed abruptly, but did not form in one-layer models. A 13-billion-parameter model contained heads for literal copying, translation and pattern matching, with respective prefix-matching scores of 0.75, 0.85 and 0.94, where higher scores indicate stronger attention to continuations of earlier matching patterns.

Measurements and conditions (5)

In-context Learning and Induction Heads

34 decoder-only Transformer language models (aggregate) · Measured induction-head prefix matching over training using head activation evaluators. · Models: 34 models across four model series; Training window: approximately 2.5 to 5 billion tokens; small models described elsewhere as approximately 1 to 3 billion tokens

Formation of heads scoring as induction heads by prefix matching: Induction heads form abruptly in the same window as the in-context learning improvement. (baseline: Before the window, induction heads have not yet formed abruptly; one-layer models do not form them.)

Challenges0 sources

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Induction spreads across changing sets of heads 13 studies

Copying can survive removal of individual induction heads or identified head sets. Redundancy grows with scale, while its distribution varies across architectures.

  • Induction breaks after fewer head ablations in Qwen2.5 (grouped-query attention) than Pythia (multi-head attention). S. Venkatesh, 2026 ↗
  • Late Pythia checkpoints retain copying after any single-head ablation, with greater redundancy at scale. Lei-Chao Dong, 2026 ↗
  • Removing identified induction heads barely affects copying in a routed transformer; removing routing destroys it. Kevin Taylor, 2026 ↗
Copying beyond standard attention 13 studies

State-space and hybrid models can solve synthetic induction tasks, which test copying after repeats, and associative recall, which tests retrieving associated items. Performance and generalisation to different sequence lengths vary substantially, and task success alone does not identify an induction circuit.

  • H3 matches Attention on the synthetic induction task, without identifying learned circuits. Tri Dao et al., 2022 ↗
  • Geometric state-space model keeps induction accuracy high across lengths where Selective state-space model performance declines. Umberto Casti et al., 2025 ↗
  • ReBased recalls multiple associated items more accurately than Based, but attention locates retrieval positions more precisely. Yaroslav Aksenov et al., 2024 ↗
Copying across modalities and prediction schemes 6 studies

Repeat-sensitive copying appears in biological sequence models, time-series models and diffusion language models. Its strength and responsible heads depend on architecture and available context.

  • Repeated protein and RNA sequences sharply reduce uncertainty, with effects varying across architectures. Pranav Kantroo et al., 2025 ↗
  • A few sharp Chronos heads sustain forecast structure, though few meet standard induction criteria. Anthony Bao et al., 2026 ↗
  • The diffusion language model's induction advantage depends on seeing both sides of the mask. Andy Catruna et al., 2026 ↗
Repeated-list retrieval resembles short-term memory 4 studies

Pretrained models retrieve repeated lists in an order-sensitive way that varies with training corpus, depth and position. These behavioural similarities do not by themselves establish an induction-head mechanism.

  • GPT-2 repeated-list retrieval depends strongly on training corpus and depth, with sensitivity to order. Kristijan Armeni et al., 2022 ↗
  • Later list positions show stronger retrieval, while copying trajectories correlate with benchmark trajectories. Kristijan Armeni et al., 2024 ↗
  • A contextual-memory model (CMR) fits top induction heads better than a Gaussian bell-curve baseline. Ji-An Li et al., 2024 ↗

Settings and limits

V5Training data and setup affect induction heads and how long in-context learning lasts 45130

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups find that training data and setup affect induction-head formation or how long in-context learning lasts, including controlled interventions in Pythia-14M–160M and a 1.485B decoder. Effects depend on the property and task: in one synthetic task, varying depth across 6, 12 and 18 layers had no consistent effect on how long in-context learning lasted.

Original resultOlsson et al., 2022 ↗

The original study trained models with “smeared keys”: each attention key mixed information from the current and previous tokens using a trainable mixing weight.

Using smeared keys enabled the transition to in-context learning in one-layer models and made that transition occur earlier in models with two or more layers.

Measurements and conditions (1)

In-context Learning and Induction Heads

Smeared-key models (aggregate) · Trained models with keys interpolated between the current token's key and the previous token's key using a trainable parameter. · Architecture: smeared key; Depth: one layer and two or more layers

Development and timing of in-context learning: In-context learning forms in one-layer models and forms earlier in two-layer and larger models. (baseline: Without smeared keys, the one-layer models do not develop the reported in-context learning transition; deeper models develop it later.)

Results, Figure 6 discussion

Challenges0 sources

No sources in this group.

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Data and architecture shape small-model in-context learning 8 studies

Depth, architecture and training-data structure affect whether small models improve with context. Task hierarchy and clustering of related examples (burstiness) also change the model scale or training needed for in-context learning.

  • Loss improvement with context depends on model depth, training progress and synthetic data entropy (randomness). Naomi Sagan et al., 2025 ↗
  • Deeper task hierarchies need larger models for in-context learning; errors fall more slowly with scale. Sushant Mehta et al., 2025 ↗
  • No evaluated architecture learns Omniglot in-context learning from purely non-bursty training; emergence timing varies. Ivan Lee et al., 2023 ↗
Induction patterns can survive further training 5 studies

Instruction tuning and continued training often preserve head-level induction or retrieval patterns. Multimodal and task-specific training can strengthen induction alongside in-context learning performance.

  • Base and instruction-tuned models retain highly correlated per-head induction scores. N. Aljaafari et al., 2026 ↗
  • Retrieval-head patterns persist across model variants but differ substantially between families. Wenhao Wu et al., 2024 ↗
  • Multimodal training and Qwen fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation strengthen induction; previous-token strength stays flat. Yi-Ran Huang et al., 2026 ↗
Induction heads can persist after in-context learning fades 4 studies

In-context learning can fade while training loss continues to improve and induction heads persist. Changes in earlier computations and competition with overall statistics learned in the weights can change what these heads do.

  • In-context learning can fade after emerging despite falling training loss, suggesting competition with weight-based learning. Aaditya K. Singh et al., 2023 ↗
  • Induction heads persist after in-context learning fades; altered earlier attention enables a strategy without such learning. Aaditya K. Singh et al., 2025 ↗
  • Next-token predictions balance pattern frequencies in context against pretrained statistics of consecutive token pairs. Shuo Wang et al., 2024 ↗
Training data shapes copying 4 studies

Repeated-data training can impair copying, and copying remains weak in a child-scale training setting. Evaluations across repetition levels must distinguish test-distribution changes from changes to training.

  • Training on repeated data sharply reduces copying recurring names in a one-layer attention-only model. Danny Hernandez et al., 2022 ↗
  • An attention-and-convolution model trained on BabyLM’s small corpus copies a repeated second half only weakly. Josh Taylor, 2026 ↗
  • Copying tests measure generalisation across repetition levels after training at a single repetition setting. Dan Friedman et al., 2024 ↗

How it works

V1Induction heads copy continuations by combining with earlier heads attending to previous tokens 46180

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups support this mechanism in small two-layer attention-only transformers, including evidence from blocking attention to the previous token during training. In language models, the order in which heads form is observed rather than experimentally tested, and path patching—intervening on specific connections between model components—shows that the simple circuit explains only part of induction behavior.

Related findings9 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Induction beyond single-token matching 15 studies

Small transformers learn induction over longer histories and copying delays selected by context. The depth and head capacity required depend on the task and architectural assumptions.

  • Multi-token induction needs more layers or first-layer heads when earlier attention uses positions alone. Nived Rajaraman et al., 2024 ↗
  • Three-layer attention learns copying delays selected by context, while tested two-layer configurations fail. Francesco D'Angelo et al., 2025 ↗
  • Sufficient heads and dimensions let two-layer attention approximate induction over multi-token contexts. Mingze Wang et al., 2024 ↗
Induction heads specialise and share functions 10 studies

Induction heads differ in prefix-length preferences and contextual selectivity. A single head can support many token-specific induction features alongside unrelated functions.

  • GPT-2 Small induction heads differ in whether they need long prefixes for strong matching. Connor Kissane et al., 2024 ↗
  • Llama2-7b induction heads attend to context-licensed repeats in disjunctions but not list controls. Sasha Boguraev et al., 2026 ↗
  • One induction head supports suffix-specific induction features and non-induction code-completion features. Connor Kissane et al., 2024 ↗
Previous-token heads support several computations 8 studies

Previous-token attention emerges in a similar training window across tested Pythia models, although its timing and layer placement vary. These heads also support computations beyond induction.

  • Previous-token attention emerges earlier and more strongly in larger Pythia models, with varying layer placement. Sean Trott, 2026 ↗
  • Previous-token heads appear in GPT2-Small indirect object identification routes, ranking highly in Llama 2-7B layers. Javier Ferrando et al., 2024 ↗
  • Previous-token-head ablation disrupts graph geometry represented from context; induction-head ablation preserves it. Andy Arditi, 2026 ↗
Induction over relations, functions and categories 8 studies

Pretrained models show induction-like matching over semantic relations, functions and categories. Interventions link some of these patterns to task performance beyond exact token copying.

  • Previous-token heads feed function-induction heads whose ablation destroys Gemma-2 9B off-by-one addition contrast accuracy. Qinyuan Ye et al., 2025 ↗
  • Multiple InternLM2-1.8B heads represent semantic relations more strongly than baselines using unrelated target entities. Jie Ren et al., 2024 ↗
  • Llama-3-8B heads match word categories, and blocking that pattern harms few-shot accuracy. Joy Crosbie et al., 2025 ↗
Copying depends on content and direction 7 studies

Copying accuracy falls with a token-rarity proxy, while induction-head attribution drops for sufficiently altered repeats. Backward-copy attention remains weak even under explicit backward-copy training.

  • Random-token copying accuracy falls with tokenizer index, a proxy for token rarity. Jingcheng Niu et al., 2025 ↗
  • Backward-copy attention remains near zero even with explicit backward-copy training. Mohammed Sabry et al., 2025 ↗
  • Induction attribution drops sharply beyond substitution thresholds that increase with repeat length. Gal Kesten-Pomeranz et al., 2026 ↗
Upstream circuits support induction in full transformers 6 studies

Induction in pretrained full transformers depends on earlier computations involving previous tokens and duplicate tokens. Damage from ablating random heads can obscure which head sets matter, and tests for selectivity can miss necessary heads.

  • Previous-token head ablation nearly eliminates induction accuracy; random-head ablation also hurts, weakening attribution, especially in OLMoE. Yongzhong Xu, 2026 ↗
  • Removing induction or previous-token paths sharply reduces GPT2-small agreement with original induction outputs. Hang Chen et al., 2024 ↗
  • OLMoE induction needs duplicate-token heads, including one never identified as induction-selective. Yongzhong Xu, 2026 ↗
Architectural shortcuts to induction 6 studies

Shifting or mixing adjacent keys and values can enable induction in one layer or accelerate learning. Other architectural changes preserve copying while changing which projections carry it.

  • Convolving keys or values lets one-layer attention solve multi-query associative recall; query-only convolution fails. Destiny Okpekpe et al., 2025 ↗
  • One-layer attention shifting keys and values represents induction exactly, learning faster than two-layer standard attention. Mingyu Xu et al., 2024 ↗
  • Without value/output projections, the loss bump accompanying induction persists, copying improves and attention keys matter more. Goutham Nalagatla et al., 2026 ↗
MLP neurons read induction-head outputs 3 studies

Induction heads feed downstream neurons associated with confidence and repetition. Head ablations reduce these neurons' activity, while repetition-neuron ablations impair recall.

  • Joint induction-head ablation lowers GPT-2 Small entropy-neuron activity toward its level when text first appears. Alessandro Stolfo et al., 2024 ↗
  • Ablating late repetition neurons harms recall; ablating induction heads lowers those neurons’ activity. Nhi Hoai Doan et al., 2025 ↗
  • Induction-head ablation reduces entropy-neuron magnitudes during decoding with retrieved information more than random-head ablation. A. Kuleshova et al., 2026 ↗
Induction-like patterns with frozen or random weights 3 studies

Transformers with frozen random weights can develop induction-like attention after training their embeddings (the vectors representing input tokens), and previous-token signals can help random models match a current token sequence to earlier occurrences. Attention that ignores the input still performs poorly on tasks that require induction.

  • Training only token embeddings produces induction-like attention patterns in a two-layer transformer with frozen random weights. Zi-Qian Zhong et al., 2024 ↗
  • Previous-token output patching raises random-model prefix matching; many top HAPAX heads suppress copied tokens. Kerem Şahin et al., 2025 ↗
  • Random attention ignoring inputs sharply harms induction-dependent tasks while preserving performance on algorithmic tasks and memorisation. Yihe Dong et al., 2025 ↗
V3Do induction heads explain most loss improvement across token positions in large transformers? 782

Suggested status ?unclear

Independent studies support a causal role for induction heads in reducing loss on later tokens relative to earlier tokens. Whether they explain most of this improvement in large transformers remains an open question.

This version's level changed from C to ?, meaning it cannot yet be decided: the two results behind the earlier C hold only under particular conditions and are neither a failed replication nor evidence that the effect is an artifact. One of them still has to be checked against the full paper, and some experiments that measure loss by token position have not yet been assessed for this version.

Original resultOlsson et al., 2022 ↗

The authors ablated (disabled) individual attention heads in small models both with MLPs (feedforward layers) and without them.

The original study attributed almost all in-context learning—learning from the current context—in small attention-only models to induction heads. In models with MLPs (feedforward layers), the evidence was suggestive but not conclusive.

Appendix A.5, Figure A15

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Retrieval heads support context-dependent answers 4 studies

Small sets of retrieval or induction-like heads causally support long-context retrieval, many-shot classification and verbatim recall. Comparisons with interventions on random heads show that the importance of targeting these particular heads varies by task.

  • Masking sparse retrieval heads harms retrieval and extractive question answering more than masking random heads. Wenhao Wu et al., 2024 ↗
  • Masking top retrieval heads nearly eliminates in-context learning accuracy on Banking77-en-ICL in a model resembling LLaMA2. Kai Hua et al., 2025 ↗
  • Induction-head ablation collapses in-order list recall in Qwen and substantially reduces it in Llama-I. Anooshka Bajaj et al., 2026 ↗
Induction interventions change how loss improves across context positions 3 studies

Suppressing or ablating induction-like heads can make loss fall less from earlier to later context positions. Stronger signs of induction-like behaviour do not necessarily mean greater causal dependence on these heads.

  • Penalising attention to tokens following earlier matches lowers the in-context learning score in two-layer GPT2. Tatsuya Aoyama et al., 2025 ↗
  • Synthetic-copy training strengthens signs of induction but makes ablation less damaging than using natural data alone. Mohammed Sabry et al., 2025 ↗
  • Ablating CMR-like heads weakens loss reductions across context more than random ablation in most tested models. Ji-An Li et al., 2024 ↗
V6Other mechanisms can carry most few-shot task learning 1273

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups find that few-shot task learning—learning a task from a few examples in context—relies mainly on heads or mechanisms other than induction heads under the conditions tested. Ablating (disabling) induction heads still impairs classification and speech tasks, so the conclusion depends on the task, which heads are selected and how they are ablated.

Original resultOlsson et al., 2022 ↗

The original paper did not test this claim.

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Label copying helps classification and causes errors 11 studies

Heads that attend to demonstration labels retrieve those labels and can supply useful task vectors, representations of the task. The same behaviour can follow incorrect labels or place too much weight on the most recent demonstration.

  • With permuted labels, disabling GPT-J heads matching same-class prefixes brings correct- and incorrect-label accuracies closer. Danny Halawi et al., 2023 ↗
  • Injecting summed induction-head outputs as task vectors sharply improves Llama2-70B zero-shot classification. Hao-Lin Yang et al., 2025 ↗
  • Correct demonstrations can lower vision-language model accuracy as predictions shift toward the latest demonstration's label. Mohammad Rostami, 2026 ↗
Mechanisms beyond copying 7 studies

Abstractive recall and graph inference involve feed-forward networks or internal representations beyond direct copying. Dialogue demonstrations can also remain useful after their sequential structure is disrupted.

  • Removing upper feed-forward sublayers harms abstractive one-shot accuracy more sharply than extractive accuracy. Jack Merullo et al., 2023 ↗
  • Swapping late-layer activations at the last token recovers most of Llama-3.1-8B's contrast between graph families. Katharine Kowalyshyn et al., 2026 ↗
  • Dialogue demonstrations retain benefits over context alone after both turns and tokens are shuffled. Jiashu Pu et al., 2024 ↗
V7Induction heads can form through several ordered stages 1761

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several studies report successive steps in induction-head formation, including in a 3M attention-only language model and Pythia/OLMo training checkpoints. The observations do not always distinguish separate transitions, and evidence that heads in larger models begin participating at different times comes from one training run per model.

Original resultOlsson et al., 2022 ↗

No original study is linked for this claim.

Section 3.2; Appendix C.2, Figure 17

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Induction within a broader developmental sequence 10 studies

Induction can precede function-vector heads and attention sinks, with some heads changing roles during training. The apparent sharpness of later abilities also depends on label semantics.

  • Many eventual function-vector heads first show induction scores, which decline as function-vector scores rise. Kayo Yin et al., 2025 ↗
  • Attention sinks form later than induction, with transition sharpness varying across model families. Yongzhong Xu, 2026 ↗
  • Symbolic labels separate abrupt first-token translation gains from gradual second-token gains; semantic labels erase this. Sultan M. Daniels et al., 2025 ↗
Simple statistical solutions can precede contextual learning 5 studies

Models can first learn individual-token frequencies (unigrams) or corpus-wide frequencies of token pairs (global bigrams) before acquiring richer mechanisms that use context. Some configurations remain at these simpler solutions.

  • Multilayer models trained on first-order Markov data plateau at unigram loss before reaching bigram solutions. A. Makkuva et al., 2024 ↗
  • Global bigram statistics are learned faster than the in-context induction mechanism during joint training. A. Bietti et al., 2023 ↗
  • Pythia 12B improves loss with context earlier on unigrams than maximum-entropy (maximally unpredictable) bigram sequences. Nora Belrose et al., 2024 ↗

Detecting induction heads

Induction scores and measurements taken during training help detect induction circuits. Their usefulness for prediction and causal evidence varies.

Signals around circuit formation 11 studies

Circuit formation shows up in measurements of loss-landscape shape, sensitivity to perturbations and spectral structure. Some signals precede changes in induction scores, while others accompany behaviour without predicting which head will emerge.

  • Measured sensitivities to induction attention patterns rise slowly, then accelerate during training. George Wang et al., 2025 ↗
  • RoPE spectral changes accompany previous-token behaviour but do not predict head identity beforehand. Heng-Yu Li, 2026 ↗
  • Participation ratio, a measure of effective dimensionality, rises before induction scores. Max Hennick et al., 2026 ↗
Induction scores can miss relevant heads 7 studies

Prefix-matching scores do not consistently identify selective or causally relevant heads. Their usefulness varies across model families and attention architectures.

  • Some GPT-2 heads retain strong key selectivity despite near-zero prefix-matching scores. Kieran A. Murphy, 2026 ↗
  • Induction scores identify arithmetic copying heads above chance in Gemma and Llama, but not Qwen. Ming Liu, 2026 ↗
  • Tests for striped attention patterns miss previous-token heads in some models; disabling them reveals their role. Realmbird, 2026 ↗

Repetition and prompt echo

Copy-related heads can contribute to unwanted repetition and prompt echo. Intervening on them has different effects across models.

Copy heads influence repetition and prompt echo 5 studies

Copy-related heads contribute to prompt echo and degenerate repetition in instruction-tuned models. Removing these heads can have the opposite effect on local repetition in GPT-2 small.

  • Disabling heads with high prefix-matching scores nearly eliminates prompt echo in small instruction-tuned models. Inez Okulska et al., 2026 ↗
  • Copying heads gain causal influence during repetition; scaling them down improves following requested repetition lengths. Shuxun Wang et al., 2025 ↗
  • Induction-head ablation increases GPT-2 small’s nearby-text repetition; restoring head activity largely reverses this. Arjun Rao, 2026 ↗

Where to start reading

  1. 1

    Catherine Olsson et al., 2022 ↗ In-context Learning and Induction Heads

    Establishes the original induction-head account, its training transition, small-model causal evidence and limits at larger scales.

  2. 2

    Kayo Yin et al., 2025 ↗ Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?

    Separates contributions from induction heads and function vectors (task representations); conclusions depend on in-context learning measures and head selection.

  3. 3

    Hao-Lin Yang et al., 2025 ↗ Unifying Attention Heads and Task Vectors via Hidden State Geometry in In-Context Learning

    Reports strong classification effects from disabling induction heads; random controls leave uncertainty about whether these effects are specific to induction.

Known gaps in this draft

Uncertainty remains about whether effects are specific to induction heads, how results depend on the measure used, how independent replications are, how training data matters and whether circuit formation has distinct stages.

All 6 gaps
  • Studies disagree on whether Pythia-160M shows functioning induction behavior. The study reporting its absence lacks random controls matched to the induction-head intervention, uncertainty estimates and a stated model checkpoint (training snapshot).
  • Disabling randomly selected attention heads can also cause large classification losses, so it remains unclear whether the effects are specific to disabling induction heads. Classification accuracy and changes in loss from earlier to later tokens measure different aspects of performance and need separate interpretations.
  • Evidence that loss still improves on samples whose answers cannot be copied from context when induction behavior is suppressed rests on a main comparison with one random seed per condition. Numerical values in the relevant figures have not all been fully verified.
  • Apparent replication across papers may involve overlapping author groups, models or training runs. Independent support for how heads combine into circuits and for patterns in how they form during training remains unclear.
  • It remains unclear how the choice of tokenizer, which splits text into tokens, affects induction heads. Existing comparisons between training corpora still leave a need for controlled comparisons with matched evaluation conditions.
  • Circuit formation within the same training window can still proceed through ordered stages. Existing interpretations do not consistently distinguish events that share a training window from events that form a single transition.
